# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 59 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 59 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_059_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 5, Part 5 — The Allegorical Key to the Parable

**59:1** I asked him further to explain all the parables and visions I had seen. He said to me: "In all the matters that I am about to show you, I will provide explanation. Only give me your complete attention of heart and mind, and everything I tell you will be clarified."

**59:2** "The field," he said, "is this world. The lord of the field is the one who created all things, brought them to completion, and empowered them. The son is the Holy Spirit. The slave is the Son of God. The vine is the people whom he planted. The fences are the holy angels of the Lord who keep his people. The weeds pulled from the vineyard are the transgressions of the servants of God. The foods sent from the feast are the commandments that he gave to his people through his Son. The friends and counselors are the holy angels who were created first. And the absence of the master is the time remaining before his coming."

**59:3** I said to him: "Lord, all these things are great and marvelous and glorious. Could I have perceived them by myself?" He said to me: "No one who has God in his heart would have hesitated to ask, nor would he have failed to receive the explanation. But I will speak with you."

**59:4** "Hear now. The slave whom the master approved and made the principal heir of all his goods — that is the Son of God. The counselors are the first-created angels. The absence of the master denotes the time remaining before his coming. The vine that is cultivated is the people of God. The fences are the angels who guard the people. The weeds pulled out are the sins of the servants. The foods sent from the feast are the commandments given to the people through the Son. The friends are the holy prophets who served God."

---

*LOGOS renders according to the Greek text of P.Mich. 130 with attention to formal correspondence and the systematic allegorical interpretation.*
